transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-25 16:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tom Huang (Catalyst AI - Head of ML), Maya Singh (Catalyst AI - Infra Lead), Jordan Lee (Product)

Summary: short discovery to understand Catalyst's p95 latency needs, concurrency and desire to compare hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments. Discussed benchmarks, streaming behaviors, and security/compliance checklist.

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll do quick intros then get into your latency and throughput needs. I'm Alex Carter, AE on the Redwood side.
[00:12] Tom: hey Alex, Tom here. We're excited to chat. I'm head of ML at Catalyst.
[00:15] Maya: Maya here, infra lead. We'll be doing the benchmarking and ops integration.
[00:20] Jordan: Jordan from product, hi.
[00:25] Priya: Priya Nair, platform SE, I'll cover benchmarks and technical tradeoffs.
[00:30] Alex: great. The goal today — capture p95 targets, concurrency, streaming requirements and which deployment mode you think you'll pilot. Tom, can you share current SLOs?
[00:41] Tom: yeah, so our ideal p95 for text-generation is around 120ms for short responses (under 256 tokens) and for longer context 300ms-ish is acceptable. Concurrency targets are, um, we expect up to 200 concurrent active sessions during peak, but that could spike.
[01:05] Maya: to add, our infra currently runs A100s and we're testing H100s in staging. We'll need VPC connectivity and strict egress controls — can't send raw logs to third-party.
[01:20] Priya: ok makes sense. When you say p95 120ms, is that cold calls or warm? Are you including network hop?
[01:28] Tom: good question — that's warm, from our edge into the model. We can accept 30-40ms network overhead. So Redwood runtime would need p95 of ~80-90ms ideally.
[01:40] Alex: got it. So for hosted vs dedicated: hosted is fastest to get started, but dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput. Private on-prem is available if you need full control.
[01:53] Tom: what's the delta in p95 between hosted and dedicated in practice?
[01:56] Priya: variable but typical differences are small if hosted capacity is in-region. For small sequence lengths (<=512) we've seen p95 reductions by tuning batching and kernel selection. For dedicated you can reduce jitter and get more consistent tail latency because of isolation — especially at high concurrency.
[02:18] Maya: how do you measure p95 exactly? Is it end-to-end including our proxies?
[02:22] Priya: Redwood measures token generation time within the runtime; you can capture end-to-end via the SDK. For benchmarking we'll provide both internal runtime p95 and end-to-end samples. Note: KV caching and prefix caching can dramatically reduce tokens/sec cost and lower latency for repeated prefixes.
[02:40] Tom: we have lots of repeated prompts in our chat flows so prefix caching sounds helpful — any rough numbers?
[02:46] Priya: varies, but for repeated instruction sets you could see 30-60% token reduction. For latency, cache hits bypass large parts of the decode path, so p95 can drop notably.
[02:58] Jordan: we also need streaming; we want partial tokens as soon as possible for UI snappiness. Does Redwood support chunked streaming with backpressure?
[03:06] Priya: yes, streaming is supported. We expose server-sent events / websocket streaming. Backpressure is managed via flow control — small tokens stream quickly but there is a tradeoff: many concurrent streams increases open connections and impacts throughput.
[03:25] Alex: what are your target tokens/sec for peak?
[03:27] Tom: we estimate about 15k tokens/sec aggregated at peak, with most requests being short (avg 40 tokens).
[03:35] Priya: good to know. For that workload we typically recommend a dedicated pool for predictable throughput; hosted can handle it but depending on SLAs and burst, dedicated simplifies SLO guarantees.
[03:48] Maya: security wise — SOC 2, SSO, KMS for key management. We need audit logs and the ability to disable logging for sensitive prompts.
[03:58] Alex: Redwood supports SOC 2 artifacts, SAML SSO, RBAC, and you can opt-out of telemetry for certain routes. KMS/HSM integrations are supported for Private deployments; hosted supports customer-managed keys in many regions. We'll share docs.
[04:12] Tom: about benchmarks — we want you to run p95 experiments for 512 and 8k sequences and a streaming scenario. Also tokens/sec for both short and long tails.
[04:21] Priya: ok we'll run three benchmark profiles: short (<=128), mid (<=512), long (8k context with KV cache enabled/disabled). We'll measure p50/p95/p99, and tokens/sec, and include GPU utilization.
[04:33] Tom: do you include warmup and steady-state windows? We care about steady-state p95.
[04:37] Priya: yes we'll include warmup and report steady-state windows; for streaming we'll measure partial-first-byte times and time-to-last-token.
[04:46] Maya: curious about autoscaling and bursting — if we hit 200->400 concurrent, how fast can Redwood provision extra capacity?
[04:55] Alex: Dedicated pools support configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity options. Typical scale-up for GPU-backed capacity is minutes, but we've built policies to keep warm spare capacity to reduce scale latency. Private on-prem depends on your infra.
[05:09] Tom: for our SLAs we need graceful degradation — if a model is unavailable it should fallback to a smaller variant. Do you support automatic fallback routing?
[05:17] Priya: yes, smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants or a lower-capacity tier. We'll help set up canaries and A/B rollouts.
[05:25] Jordan: pricing? we need cost per token estimates for hosted vs dedicated committed monthly.
[05:30] Alex: we'll send a detailed sheet but in short: hosted billing per-token with volume tiers; dedicated is reserved capacity (commitment) with lower per-token economics plus burst pricing. We'll include example run-rate math for your 15k tokens/sec peak.
[05:46] Tom: great. A few technical clarifications — do you support quantized model runtimes? we want to test fp16 vs int8 for cost/perf tradeoffs.
[05:55] Priya: yes, the runtime supports quantization-friendly paths and we'll recommend quant profiles based on your workload. For some models int8 gives big cost reductions with modest quality loss; we'll include quality monitoring.
[06:07] Maya: about networking — for Private/VPC we need enforced egress rules and on-prem air-gapped option.
[06:14] Alex: Private supports customer-managed networking, optional on-prem package for air-gapped environments, and KMS/HSM integrations. We'll attach the deployment checklist.
[06:24] Tom: can you share an example benchmark result for a model with similar load?
[06:28] Priya: yes — I can share recent internal results. For example, for 512-seq with H100 and Redwood optimizations we saw p95 around 85-100ms at 100 concurrent streams and tokens/sec ~5k for that instance mix. For 8k seq numbers vary a lot, p95 moves into the several hundreds ms range depending on batch size.
[06:51] Jordan: what about tokenization and prompt prep — do you offload tokenization or is it on client?
[06:56] Priya: tokenization can be on client or server; for consistent measurements we recommend server-side tokenization during benchmarks to reflect true end-to-end. Note tokenization adds a few ms for short prompts.
[07:08] Tom: any gotchas — like cold starts for KV cache?
[07:11] Priya: KV cache warmup occurs on first full-context runs. For chat flows with repeated prefixes, we show improvement after first few requests. We'll simulate steady-state in benchmarks.
[07:22] Maya: about observability — we need per-route breakdown and token-level cost.
[07:27] Alex: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-model dashboards, traces and error analysis. We can add your routes to the dashboard during trial.
[07:36] Tom: ok next steps — can you run the benchmarks and we provide the harness?
[07:40] Priya: yes, we'll need your harness or we can use our test harness and you'll validate. For the pilot we'd like: test scripts, sample prompts, SLOs and a list of endpoints to exercise.
[07:51] Maya: we'll send a harness. Also timeline — we are aiming for a pilot in early April, and production decision by end of Q2.
[07:59] Alex: sounds good. We'll aim to have benchmark results and pricing before your pilot.
[08:05] Tom: on failover, do you keep audit logs of fallback events?
[08:09] Priya: yes, audit logs include routing decisions, model fallbacks, and error traces. Logs are available in console and via export.
[08:18] Jordan: any mention of competitors? we run small PoCs with Anthropic and self-host attempts.
[08:23] Alex: that's common; we'll show economics and latency comparisons where possible.
[08:28] Tom: ok thanks, one last — want to clarify metrics for streaming: first-byte latency p95 target is 60ms?
[08:35] Priya: for short streaming messages 60ms p95 is aggressive but achievable in-region with tuned stacks and warm caches — we'll test and report measured numbers.
[08:47] Maya: for the benchmark, collect: p50/p95/p99, time-to-first-byte, time-to-last-token, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and memory footprints.
[08:58] Priya: noted. We'll also include the kernel selection and quant profile used.
[09:05] Alex: Great. Quick recap and owners.
[09:09] Priya: I'll run the three benchmark profiles and share results.
[09:13] Alex: I'll send pricing and security docs.
[09:16] Maya: I'll send infra baseline and the harness.
[09:19] Tom: we'll review and set the follow-up.
[09:22] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll sync up next week.

End of call.
